Journal entry review

Reads every entry in a period, scores the manual ones against risk indicators, says which tests it could not run, and changes nothing in the books.

Watch someone use it

Example run with fictional figures: Northbrook Trading, every journal entry, 1 July to 30 September 2026. The figures match the worked examples on the step-by-step page.

Claudewith the MosoFin journal entry review skill

Can you review our journal entries for the third quarter before the audit committee meets?

Claude

Yes. Before I read anything, I need nine answers. I ask them all at once, so the run does not stop again for each one.

  1. Do you want me to use MosoFin, or will you upload the data?
  2. Which period do I review?
  3. What are your approval limits? I never assume one.
  4. Optional: what size of amount is material for you?
  5. Does anyone make adjustments outside the books, for example your accountant at year end, in tax software or in a spreadsheet?
  6. Who may see the output? It names logins and entries.
  7. Must someone approve a hand-typed entry? If yes, can you export who approved each one?
  8. Through which date are the books closed, and when was the close done?
  9. Optional: which accounts are sensitive, and do you know of any risk areas?

Use MosoFin. 1 July to 30 September. The owner approves hand-typed entries over $10,000 by email, but we keep no export. Materiality is $25,000. Our outside accountant keeps year-end adjustments in a consolidation workbook. Output for the CFO and the audit committee. Books closed through 30 September, close done 9 October. Revenue, deferred revenue, the warranty reserve and equity are sensitive.

Claude

Here is my plan. I review every journal entry that Northbrook Trading posted from 1 July to 30 September, against a baseline from the six prior quarters. The approval limit is $10,000 and materiality is $25,000.

The adjustments in the consolidation workbook are not in this population. You keep no approval log, so I report the four approval tests as not run. The output is for the CFO and the audit committee. Shall I start?

Yes, go ahead.

Claude

I read 1,284 transactions of all types. A person typed 48 of them by hand, which is 3.7%. Each one has a transaction date, a create date, a login and a description. Before I screen them, I prove that I read them all:

Tie-out
Debits of the 1,284 transactions I read$2,486,310.45
= General ledger movement for the quarter$2,486,310.45

The difference is 0.00, so the screen is complete. The adjustments in the consolidation workbook are not in it, and the report header says so.

Claude

I start with the pattern, because it matters more than any one entry. In three quarters in a row, the owner login released the warranty reserve by hand on a Saturday:

Pattern: warranty reserve releases, account 2450
QuarterReleaseOperating profit after
Q1, Sat 28 Mar$9,500.00$50,000
Q2, Sat 27 Jun$9,700.00$50,000
Q3, Sat 26 Sep$9,800.00$50,000

Each release is just below your $10,000 limit, so none needed approval. Each one brings the quarter to exactly $50,000. In total, $29,000 left the reserve. This is a question, not a finding.

Claude

I screened all 1,284 transactions. Seven of the 48 hand-typed entries meet at least one warning sign. Three score 6 or more, so I review them:

Flagged entries, top three
EntryScoreWarning signs
JE-202609-027, $1,263.4010Dated 30 Sep, typed in 12 Oct, after the close, into a closed period
JE-202609-019, $9,800.009Reserve, just below the limit, unusual login, "adjustment", weekend, period end
JE-202609-023, $33,000.006Revenue, at or above materiality, round amount, period end

The other four flags score 2 or less, and the report states each weight. The books cannot explain these three. I ask roles, not people. Can the bookkeeper explain JE-202609-027 and JE-202609-023?

The bookkeeper says 027 is the late September utilities bill. 023 defers the Pinnacle annual contract. Receipt and contract attached.
